notes.1: Too many candidates when using v = u + at did not realise that the v value should have been negative as it is travelling downwards. Answer: 1.27s
notes.2i: By resolving horizontally and using T = λx/L, the required value of λ could be found. Some candidates tried to use an energy method which was not relevant here.
notes.2iii: Many candidates found this part of the question very difficult. A 3 term energy equation was required involving 2 EE terms and 1 PE term. Answers: (i) 5 (ii) 0.8
notes.3: This question proved to be rather difficult.
notes.3i: Most candidates knew that it was necessary to take moments about O. A number of candidates used an incorrect formula to find the centre of mass of the hemi-sphere. Sign errors often appeared in the candidates equation.
notes.3iii: Candidates again knew to take moments about O. Very few correct answers were seen. The required equation should have been 24x + Wy = (24 + W)x 0.15, where x was the distance of centre of mass from part (i), y was the centre of mass of the hemi-sphere H and W the weight of H. Answers: (i) 0.225m (ii) 40N
notes.4i: Some candidates used the trajectory equation quoted in the formula booklet and so did not obey the instructions given in the question. It was necessary to use horizontal and vertical motion to set up the equations x = 10t and y = 15t – gt2. t = x/10 can then be substituted into the y expression to find the required result.
notes.4iii: This part of the question required y = –14 to be substituted into the equation found in part (i). This resulted in a quadratic equation and when solved gave the required answer. Answers: (i) y = 1.5x – 0.05x2 (ii) distance ˂ 30 (iii) 37.5m
notes.5i: The incorrect formula was used by some candidates for the centre of mass of the lamina. The distance should have been 2 × 0.7 sin(π/2)/(3π/2) and not 2 × 0.7 sin(π/2)/(π/2). The reaction at P will be perpendicular to the plane. With this in mind the candidate needed to take moments about
notes.5iii: Very few correct answers were seen. Here candidates needed to resolve horizontally and vertically for the forces acting at P and then to use tanθ = vertical force/horizontal force, where θ is the required angle. Answers: (i) 7.12N (ii) 65.6°
notes.6i: This part of the question can be solved by using T = λx/L and Newton’s Second Law horizontally with the acceleration equal to rω2. This gave the correct value of ω, the angular speed. The final step was to resolve vertically to find θ.
notes.6iii: Candidates now needed to find the required KE. Before they could do this, the velocity v had to be calculated by using v = rω. The EE can be calculated by using an extension of 0.1. Finally the difference can be found. Answers: (i) 6.32 rads−1, 60° (ii) 0.4125J
notes.7i: Candidates needed initially to work out the coefficient of friction, µ. This was µ = F/R = 0.6 × 0. 52/(0.5g) = 0.03. Newton’s Second Law can now be applied giving 0.5dv/dt = 0.6t2 – 0.03 × 0.5g. This would then give the correct equation.
notes.7iii: Candidates now had to integrate again to find the displacement. By substituting t = 0.5 and v = 0 the constant of integration was calculated. Finally t = 1.2 was used to find the required displacement. Answers: (i) dv/dt = 1.2t2 – 0.3 (ii) v = 0.4t3 – 0.3t + 0.1 (iii) 0.0926
notes.general_comments:
The paper was of a very similar standard to the one set last June.
Very few candidates now use g = 9.8 or 9.81.
Candidates should refer to the formula booklet provided if in doubt about a formula.
Some candidates are still losing marks for not giving answers to 3 significant figures and also due to
premature approximating within their calculations leading to the final answer. Candidates should be
reminded that if an answer is required to 3 significant figures then their working should be performed to at
least 4 significant figures.
The easier questions proved to be 4(ii), 4(iii), 7(i) and 7(ii)
The harder questions proved to be 2(ii), 3(i), 3(ii) and 5(ii)
